---
title: "Research"
---

My research develops computational methods and analysis frameworks for spatial transcriptomics, with a focus on making imaging-based single-cell measurements trustworthy before they're interpreted.

## Cell segmentation quality in spatial transcriptomics

Imaging-based spatial platforms like 10x Xenium assign millions of transcripts to individual cells — but every downstream conclusion depends on how well cell boundaries were drawn. I develop **CRISP** (Co-expression Rejection In Segmentation Purity), an R package that flags cells co-expressing mutually exclusive marker genes to quantify segmentation errors without ground-truth annotation.

Using CRISP, I'm benchmarking segmentation algorithms — including the 10x segmentation kit, Baysor, Proseg, and Segger — across a multi-organ mouse tissue atlas, asking which methods hold up in which tissue contexts.

## Xenium analysis pipelines

Alongside the benchmarking work, I've built an open-source toolchain for Xenium experiments: Nextflow pipelines for generating alternative segmentations, Seurat-based workflows for QC through annotation, and utilities for splitting and processing tissue microarrays. These are described on the [software page](software.qmd).

## Earlier work: epigenetics of immune memory

During my PhD I studied how transcriptomic and epigenomic states define human memory T cell subsets, using integrated RNA-seq and ATAC-seq. We identified chromatin regions whose accessibility before and after activation (*poised accessible regions*) distinguishes memory subsets and their activation potential.
